item.title: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
item.description: 217 points, 36 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (haddyalchaer.com)

→ HN comments  ·  217 points  ·  36 comments

Top #1 — robotresearcher:

There’s a repeated theme here that I don’t understand. For example:

> (3) That's where I decided to build a harder test, where each task takes its start from one demonstration and its goal from another

> (4) I also built an interactive demo where I could place the block anywhere and pick any goal. [but] The goals in the harder test are frames from expert demonstrations

Why lean so hard on the demonstration examples? Surely the actual task here is to move between any two arbitrary poses.

So if the demonstration set is statistically strange in any way, you keep banging into that. And even if you get great results, you still haven’t shown that it generalizes to the generic system. And the one thing you know 100% about a physical robot system is that you will never encounter exactly the same situation twice.

Is there actually a reason to pick eval examples from the demonstrations instead of independent samples from the underlying task?

I’m pretty sure that the T-shoving problem doesn’t have goal reachability issues. And if it did, test 4 could run into them since the start pose is arbitrary.

↳ reply — nightpool:

Agreed, I don't know much about JEPA but i wish this article had explained / motivated the memory graph more. "3. Fill gaps in memory with transformed memories" in particular seemed really really damning for the models—when you removed the examples from the demonstration that were near the goal state, the model completely broke. It seems like the only way you could make the model work again would be to manually flip and transform the memories it did have so there was something in the vicinity of the goal location.

That seems like a really massive failure of the model to generalize? This doesn't seem like a new technique, it seems like you've discovered a pretty big issue with the fundamental setup

Top #2 — hazrmard:

JEPA is very similar to Model Predictive Control. Here, you swap the model of the system with black-box simulator (a neural net), apply some version of dynamic programming / Bellman equation to find the optimal action over planning horizon.

In the planning stage, by factoring out the optimization step from the rollout step, you can free the model to focus on learning the dynamics in latent space. (The other case, where the rollout+optimization happen in the learning loop, just becomes model-free RL.)

My background straddles classical & data-driven controls. This was the first similarity that popped out to me when I first started learning about world models.

Is JEPA just MPC but where the "M" is a latent-space model?

Top #3 — reasonabl_human:

Hands-on learning is an awesome thing - especially in the age of AI!

But maybe worth reframing away from “discovering” - hierarchical planning, sub-goals, action chunking etc. are well understood - this is more of a… transcript of your personal learning journey?

Which is still cool to see. But I read through expecting there to be some kind of novel results. We probably need to categorize these kinds of posts a bit better.

↳ reply — wilkystyle:

Hm, I get your perspective, but completely disagree with your expectation. I'm not sure I would be entitled to expect a discovery that is novel with regard to current scientific knowledge unless I'm reading a paper. The fact that it is couched as "I discovered" and posted to a personal blog should be more than enough to convey that you might not find novel scientific discoveries within.

↳↳ reply — reasonabl_human:

Fair. To clarify, I jumped in seeing this ranked #1 on HN which warped my expectations.

The root of my concern is the overall trend I'm seeing on HN: Someone spends time iterating with a coding agent exploring a field that's new to them. The agent's suggestions come from existing literature, but it rarely says "this is Search on the Replay Buffer, here's the paper." So each new concept feels like a discovery and gets written up that way. The enthusiastic tone of AI-assisted writing adds to this sensationalized effect.

So my concrete feedback would be a title like "Learnings from 600 planning experiments with LeWM on Push-T" since the current one suggests something novel about JEPA world models in general. And cite techniques they've learned along the way so others can learn from source material too.

item.title: OpenAI disbands its robotics team as its general models start running robots
item.description: 143 points, 64 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (fortune.com)

→ HN comments  ·  143 points  ·  64 comments

Top #1 — jacquesm:

General models can run robots. They are very bad at it. It is much more efficient to have a stack of models with 'dumber' but faster models taking care of lower level functions and higher level ones that are much slower taking care of high level planning. Consciousness isn't super fast, but it is very smart. Your 'lizard brain' (to use an overstretched metaphor) and reflexive system are relatively stupid but far faster and condense a whole raft of inputs to something your consciousness can deal with. For robots it isn't all that different. Sensors and actuators require millisecond level responses, that's something you're not going to get out of an LLM on the other side of a communications link.

↳ reply 1 — mrtksn:

What models actually run? Do they generate the PWM signals/their widths to drive a servo or something? Or is it more like "joystick commands" generator?

↳↳ reply — jacquesm:

More like high level motion controller, so 'servo 23 1700 us' or for better grade servos 'servo 23 pos 145400', possibly concurrent with motion commands to other actuators and possibly synchronized, possibly using other kinds of protocols (G-codes).

Motion controllers are pretty impressive these days. PWM generation is too time critical to leave to high level processors, usually this is done in hardware if you want it to be guaranteed glitch free but there are also 'bit banging' servo controllers out there.

↳↳↳ reply — mrtksn:

Interesting, so how does the inference work here? are they aiming for a fixed length intervals like 10 times/second generating the positions or is it more like reactive, i.e when the request to hold a cup from a higher level comes then this is treated as a promt, the sensors are the context and when the inference finished the pulses are sent according to the output?

↳ reply 2 — gopalv:

> Sensors and actuators require millisecond level responses, that's something you're not going to get out of an LLM on the other side of a communications link.

We've gotten to slightly a frame behind for the models I'm using to play video games - 36ms to get the next action.

The idea is probably not have a frontier model doing this, but to make a frontier model build these out of its own brain (well, directly edit the weights instead of RL tuning).

My team did call these sort of slices of a main brain a "Reflex agent" in similar fashion, since they do not reason only respond.

↳ reply 3 — baq:

> General models can run robots. They are very bad at it.

Reminder frontier labs are 6 months ahead of public models internally, if not more

the bitter lesson assumes compute is cheap and abundant, which is not really true in most robotics contexts. Unless your datacenter is right next to the robot, and you are streaming real time sensors to it.

The Bitter Lesson comes for everything eventually.

↳ reply 2 — woopsn:

item.description: 831 points, 254 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (twitter.com)

Top #1 — fweimer:

Well, OpenOffice wouldn't print on Tuesdays:

“ What a fascinating bug!! My wife has complained that open office will never print on Tuesdays!?! Then she demonstrated it. Sure enough, won't print on Tuesday. Other applications print. I think this is the same bug. Here is my guess:

Print to a postscript file. Observe the line: %%CreationDate: (Tue Mar 3 19:47:42 2009)

Change "Tue" to anything else: %%CreationDate: (XTue Mar 3 19:47:42 2009)

Save the file and it prints. Tools like evince work because they simply omit the "CreationDate" tag to begin with.

Now something odd happens when my cups script (I am using the Brother MFC420CN) copies the file to a temp file. Some of the code is rearranged, not sure how or why, but it uses a command called "file" to identify the file as "PostScript". This check would work on the original file you printed, but by the time it runs the check on the temp file, it misidentifies. Normally it would return:

   PostScript document text conforming at level 3.0
But there is another check that happens before the PostScript check. If it finds "Tue" at the fourth byte of the file, it identifies it as:

   Jan 22 14:32:44 MET 1991\011Erlang JAM file - version 4.2
So it's not a problem w/ openoffice.org, cups, or the brother printer drivers. It is a bug in the `file` utility, and documented at https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/file/+bug/248619. ”

https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/cupsys/+bug/255161...

↳ reply 1 — adrian_b:

I consider LibreOffice Writer superior to old MS Word versions, and old MS Word versions superior to new MS Word versions.

In my opinion, the quality of MS Word peaked some time in the early 2000s.

So today, given the choice between LibreOffice and MS Word, I would always choose LibreOffice, even if MS Word were free, and despite the fact that LibreOffice Writer has some annoying bugs that have not been fixed for many years, but I find easier to work around those bugs than to cope with the user interface of modern MS Word.

On the other hand, I agree that MS Excel is clearly superior to LibreOffice Calc. Nonetheless, there already are decades since I switched to LibreOffice Calc and I did not need the extra features of MS Excel. For things beyond the capabilities of Calc, I use a real database, though that would probably not be the best solution for a typical office worker.

In the distant past I liked a lot MS Access, but I have no idea whether today it is still useful. I abandoned it many years ago, after I had some problems with the migration of data between different versions of MS Access and even more with the migration of data from MS Access to another database manager.

↳↳ reply — maxerickson:

It's fairly likely that your (reasonable) complaint is that you don't know where the buttons are anymore. I edit dozens of somewhat complex documents and don't really spend much time thinking about the interface.

A big thing that came with the roll out of OOXML, along with the controversy, is that all of the weird serialization corruption bugs went away.

↳ reply 2 — StableAlkyne:

A major barrier to the improvement of giant FOSS replacements like GIMP and LibreOffice is that the people who develop it and the people who use it have become very used to all of its quirks. It's extremely hard to identify the rough edges in a UI without an external perspective.

Blender is a little different because every 3D modeling program is odd in its own way, and the new UI was close enough that it was easy to learn after the transition (I do still use the legacy keybinds though).

But Blender is very niche hobby software. To "succeed" (if we define success as capturing a significant user share from closed source spyware), Libre and GIMP need to offer workflows that are close to what the average non-coder technical person expects. Maybe that isn't valued by the teams, or maybe they don't have enough resources to make it happen, but the end result is a reputation of jank.

I dislike vibe coded clones because of concerns about the engineering quality. But the reason they're making waves when traditional FOSS hasn't is that the UX is leagues ahead.

→ HN comments  ·  163 points  ·  72 comments

Top #1 — yakkomajuri:

I'm pretty sure at this point every tax ID (CPF) in Brazil is available on a database you can get on the dark web.

We've had a "CPF-ication" of everything in Brazil over the last few years. The vast majority of people have shared this number with their local grocery store, pharmacy, gym, etc. It's required for a lot of stuff and pretty necessary for others.

Given that, if that's all that leaked here that's a pretty good outcome. It's sad that I think like this but it's kind of how it is.

What makes me more pessimistic is that they claim no financial data was exposed but I wonder if that's really true. And that's where the gold is because then scammers know who to target.

↳ reply — gchamonlive:

Many restaurants and events require CPF to open a virtual tab with an RFC card and will refuse service if you refuse to give it

Top #2 — cesarb:

For those who don't know it, our tax id (CPF) is basically public information. For instance: we just had an election. The official public site with the official information about all the candidates (https://divulgacandcontas.tse.jus.br/) has the CPF for all of them. Want to know our president's CPF? It's there.

The bad part is the rest. Having the name together with the phone number, plus being on the list meaning you most likely have one of a particular set of products from Caixa, makes it much easier for the scammers to pretend to be from the bank.

Top #3 — airstrike:

It's important to note the Brazilian tax id (CPF) is not meant to be a well kept secret like the American SSN

↳ reply — SoftTalker:

The American SSN was not originally meant to be secret either, nor used for identification other than for Social Security/Tax purposes.

But because it was a nationally unique number for every individual, it got used as a primary key for all sorts of other things, and it ended up becoming very sensitive.

↳↳ reply — samueloph:

Not disagreeing, but I think it's better to see this from a slightly different perspective:

> But because it was a nationally unique number for every individual, it got used as a primary key for all sorts of other things, and it ended up becoming very sensitive.

What makes it so sensitive is not the fact that it identifies a person and it's used everywhere, it's the fact that it's being used the wrong way. Absolutely no authentication should be done solely on the basis of the SSN. You can still have it be the primary key, but that shouldn't grant authentication by itself.

The Brazilian CPF is the same in identifying a person and being used everywhere, but it's not used a the sole mechanism of authentication as often as the SSN is used, although when it is then it ends up suffering from the same problem.

The only way to really solve this is for governments to enforce that solely knowing these types of IDs can't lead to any authentication, that's unacceptable and should be treated the same way knowing the name of a person is (which funnily enough some governments also treat it wrongly in similar ways, but you get the point).

item.title: Jonathan Blow – If AI Solved Coding, Why Is My Software Still the Same? [video]
item.description: 147 points, 134 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (youtube.com)

→ HN comments  ·  147 points  ·  134 comments

Top #1 — barbariangrunge:

Blow argues software development hasn't advanced much since the early 2000s. As a game developer, I want to offer a counter point.

In the last 3 years, there have been a lot more indie games of far higher quality than we used to get. I'm thinking of the RTS space right now. The Scouring for example. We went from having nobody but Blizzard able to make something that complex to several games with outstanding performance and complexity, often with their own custom game engines that are not only working but working better than I remember wc3/sc2 working at launch.

I don't know how much of a role AI is playing in those games, but I think the performance and complexity of indie games is shooting up and we are seeing very, very small teams make things that large teams struggled with in the past. Honestly, I think indie studios are outperforming AAA in most ways besides spend and length and art budget --and yet, it's the indies who are making their own game engines these days, isn't it?

(btw, we have to also admit that many of these game engine builders look to blow for inspiration (to carmack too), and their architectures are not what you'll find at typical saas companies. Game coding is complicated in a really fun way I didn't get doing plumbing on web projects, speaking for myself)

↳ reply 1 — corysama:

As far as the coding user experience that I have personally observed, game programming peaked with the team developing NBA Inside Drive 2004 for the Xbox.

Their workflow was:

1) Arrive at work. Get coffee. Fetch latest code from Visual Source Safe.

2) Turn on Xbox. Hit F5 to build, deploy and start debugging on target.

3) Edit and Continue C++ in debugger IDE all day on target without ever bothering to stop the game. (Yes, this took some coding discipline to maintain.)

4) Turn off Xbox and go home.

Between the Visual Studio debugger and the Whole Tomato coding assistance, it was easy to understand the code and the runtime behavior. For anything GPU-related, Microsoft Pix for Xbox gave you a scrubbable timeline of every action, every pixel, every register change in the GPU while drawing a frame.

The hardware capabilities, available libraries, and artist tools have increased tremendously since then. But, the coding experience has not. 20 years later, I'm outside of gaming and I find most people using re-run-and-printf debugging for professional development. Even locally. I don't know how anyone gets anything done.

The only significant improvements I've seen in 20 years (besides the occasional memory tracker or profiler tool) has been AI agents and reversible debuggers. Otherwise, it's all been downhill since 2004.

↳↳ reply — LugosFergus:

I haven’t used it personally, but I always heard that VSS was a complete train wreck.

Gamedev programming probably hit a low point for me when XBox One and WiiU came around. Those were some truly awful experiences.

↳↳↳ reply — barbariangrunge:

↳ reply 2 — sarchertech:

I think the majority of the improvements come from 3 places.

1. Hardware advancements mean that you can get the same results with less optimized code (this is what allowed 3rd party engines with GC scripting languages to become popular)

2. The proliferation of learning resources and open source code.

3. The budgets and size of indie studios as well as total time spent on the games. Seriously look at some of the games these days that get labeled indie.

Warcraft 1 (my first RTS) had just 4 programmers. And only one of them was on the project the whole time. And the entire project was only 14 months.

→ Article (discourse.haskell.org)

→ HN comments  ·  181 points  ·  86 comments

Top #1 — ecshafer:

I was thinking of Haskell recently, why isn't it more popular with AI? Haskell is very terse and token efficient, it has many expressive safety features. Rust is getting additional adoption because of its strictness, so hey why not have this in Rust over Javascript if it takes the same time to write?

An ideal language for agentic AI I would think is extremely strict, where the AI can iterate over the tooling for correctness. It would probably be less verbose and more terse to allow the AI to be more efficient with tokens.

↳ reply 1 — drewr:

It's my default for all the reasons you mention.

In fact if I have to ship in a different language, I'll often do a Haskell version first to steer towards isolating IO, enforcing referential transparency, and generally picking up other functional patterns that are a good idea no matter what. Then I'll port the Haskell version to whatever the solution demands.

↳↳ reply — mncharity:

> do a Haskell version first [...] port

As lower-hanging fruit, to get some style steering, but not the strictness/correctness assist in implementation, there's also doing code sketches in hs - writing without testing - and then asking for whatever code as inspired by / in the spirit of / based on the reference sketch.

↳ reply 2 — danpalmer:

> Haskell is very terse and token efficient

I'm not certain this is the case. I find AI better at producing code in languages where there are fewer abstractions. It's great at writing Go, because everything is there on the page in text/tokens, and I find it less good at writing (good) Swift, because there are lots more abstractions for it to reason about, which are not written in text/tokens on the page.

This is part of why I think LLMs producing dense and unpleasant to read text is linked to their ability, it's no coincidence that people have this criticism of all of the independently developed frontier models.

We can train around this, the frontier models are getting better at it, but it's a good reminder that LLMs are just text calculators at some level, and do much better when the concepts are in text rather than abstractions in our minds.

↳ reply 3 — calebkaiser:

I do AI research and mostly work with Lean these days. I love Haskell, though I wouldn't consider myself a particularly strong Haskell programmer (just never spent a ton of time working in it). I think you're spiritually correct that there are lots of reasons to use extremely strict languages with AI, but the reality is a little messier than you'd expect.

Token efficiency is specifically the place where strict languages get a little trickier. With dynamic languages where the model has a ton of training data, like Python, the agents are really good at writing code that just works. You still have challenges there, but they're just different than the challenges you hit with a language like Haskell/Lean/Agda etc. With Lean, for example, the amount of things the agent decides it needs to prove for a relatively trivial operation can lead to an absurd amount of code. And the way it decides to prove them can be borderline labyrinthian. It sort of plays perfectly towards current agent weaknesses, where agents can run off and reinvent a lot of machinery and build unnecessarily complex abstractions.

And those iterations have a cost. Even if the final artifact is more terse, the path to getting there can involve a huge amount of backtracking and rewriting and off-by-one syntactic corrections.

Ultimately, a lot of this comes down to developer experience. Getting useful error messages for the agent, having fast compile times so that the agent can iterate quickly, providing useful utilities for debugging, etc. There was a popular blog post specifically about Haskell that generally makes this point--the Haskell language is, in a vacuum, ideal in a lot of ways for AI, but the Haskell developer experience and ecosystem made it hard for this team to build with it via agents: https://avi.press/posts/2026-07-10-after-7-years-in-producti...

Note: I am not advocating against using these kinds of language. Obviously, I still work in Lean and a little in Agda and some related languages/projects, so I think this direction is right. Probably biased in that I love them with or without LLMs, but I do think they're also more ideal for AI development. There are still just challenges in getting agents productive in them, and most of the challenges are not about the type systems but the actual ergonomics and dev experience.

Top #2 — pmkary:

There is this memo video of S. P. Jones that famously says "Haskell is Useless". I love Haskell, but I wished it was universal like C, C++, JavaScript, Rust, and C#. By that I mean: It could be used to create apps for desktop, mobile, and web. JavaScript can be used to do so many things like power the entire web, be on node and let anyone create cli and share the code with web, and mobile through React Native, on desktop with Electron and its alike things, it lets you do plugins for god knows how many things, it lets you write things for the GNOME Shell... C and C++ are perhaps behind everything in the world and string theory finally gets seen will see they are written in C. And they can be compiled to Web and almost everything in the world. Rust is a placeholder for the two, and C# reinvented itself when it saw Mono and now works even in the browser. Each time I see Haskell I wonder what else can I do rather than creating CLI apps, and it makes me choose something else that grants me more code reuse and interesting applications.

If I could have a vision for Haskell, it was for it to be useful. Academic research and making compilers is cool, a few cli things here and there are cool too, but why can't we build music players and game engines and flutters and web pages with it? The language is way more elegant and beautiful than all the JS/C like languages out there and I really wished I could use it for the things I did. I'm aware of Servant/Yesod/IHP/Miso/Reflex for web, GTK/Monomer for desktop, TidalCycles for music, SDL/gloss for games, and various FFI/plugin, but none of them feel as coherent and worked on as the others, none of them are polished. Haskell surely needs good DX, but it also needs really better reasons for existing.

↳ reply 1 — pbrowne011:

> There is this memo video of S. P. Jones that famously says "Haskell is Useless".

I think that is an unfair characterization of the video and the intent of Haskell's co-creator, based on the rest of your comment. Simon Peyton Jones makes a graph with two dimensions, useful/useless and safe/unsafe. The question he gets at is: how can one distinguish between effectful and effect-free computations in a programming language? He proceeds to characterize most useful languages as unsafe, and Haskell as useless but safe. He then spends the majority of the video talking about how useful languages are becoming safer, and at the same time how Haskell must become useful.

https://youtu.be/iSmkqocn0oQ

↳↳ reply — raddan:

I've loved this video for years, primarily because of SPJ's willingness (and excitement, even) to talk about Haskell's shortcomings. I think SPJ and other important people in the Haskell community are keenly aware that Haskell appeals to a specific demographic and that, to survive as more than just a research plaything, that they need to broaden participation.

The famously friendly "Learn You a Haskell" book features its first "helloworld" program deep into the middle of the book, _after_ functors and (if I recall correctly) monads. It takes a very special beginner programmer to push that far through, working in the REPL, before they can write programs that do basic I/O.

I teach functional programming to college sophomores and juniors, and I would love to teach them Haskell. But I have to meet them where they are, and it would be difficult to do in Haskell. This is why we have taught either F#, Scala, or LISP over the years. F# in particular has a lot of the aesthetic qualities of Haskell while allowing impurity or mutability escape hatches without too much trouble. If somebody has truly beginner-friendly Haskell resources, I would love to hear about it-- I'm apparently not smart enough to chart that path myself.

↳ reply 2 — epgui:

> It could be used to create apps for desktop, mobile, and web

Haskell can 100% be used to create all of these kinds of apps.

The jvm world has achieved a few of these goals, and is in some ways an exemplar for these lofty goals.

Top #1 — uecker:

Zig is a nice language, but those articles always compare new languages against old-style C without use of modern tools. Most of the listed advantages you can have in C as well if you are willing to adopt modern tooling and style: signed overflow checking: sanitizers, errors you can not ignore: [[nodiscard]], slice type which know their size: variably-modified types or span types.

Defer will also appear in C compilers soon, but personally I still think goto-error handling is clearer.

(Rust has an advantage for temporal memory safety, but this does apply to Zig.)

↳ reply 1 — bunderbunder:

It seems that part of what Zig is trying to do, though, is create a pit of success around these practices. So the response might be something like, “Yes you can do these things in modern C, but doing it consistently requires more discipline than we’d like.”

https://blog.codinghorror.com/falling-into-the-pit-of-succes...

↳↳ reply — uecker:

I do not think it needs a lot of discipline. It needs the willingness to do it, but this is also true for adopting a different language.

↳ reply 2 — simjnd:

Zig's tooling is very good, so is the cross-compatibility story and tagged unions.

But while you can have some/most of the benefits Zig has from modern C, I think an underrated benefit is the language culture. As a different language it was the opportunity for a reset, e.g. it's idiomatic Zig to pass allocators to functions, meaning every library in Zig will work this way.

You could do that in C, but none or very few libraries do that so whenever you reach out to third-party dependencies (which is not a lot, in C as in Zig) you have to fight against C's traditional patterns.

↳ reply 3 — erikpukinskis:

That works as long as you have zero dependencies.

As soon as you have dependencies you are dealing with however the authors decided to build things.

Part of why languages exist is just to get a new ecosystem.

At this point, you could fork C/C++, only remove features, give it a new name, a new package service, and maybe fork the standard library, and you could end up with something pretty competitive against Zig or Rust.

Top #2 — variadix:

I’ve settled on a dialect of C++ for systems programming after using C for a long time. It’s mostly C-like and I disable exceptions, RTTI, etc. but I do use templates, overloads, methods, lambdas, etc.

I have my own object system with constructor methods that all return a status code so you don’t need exceptions, my own stdlib for containers, buffered I/O, networking, hashing, math, threading, async, etc.

C++ gives you all the features to effectively build your own language, and you can use first class tooling since C++ is widely supported. LLMs also make it much easier to build out and test an entire stdlib on your own.

↳ reply 1 — adsharma:

The reason why I prefer a GC based compiled language with types vs Rust or Zig is that they put memory allocation front end center in the language.

Sometimes I want to think about algorithms and memory management separately.

  scores = {"alice": 100, "bob": 85}
  scores["charlie"] = 92
Try translating to zig.

This is why we need natural language -> pseudo code -> GC typed -> Low level systems.

Both Zig and Rust are fine as the last stage of this software development pipeline with different trade-offs. Problems arise when people try to use them earlier in the process.

↳ reply 2 — faresahmed:

Agreed. I'd not ditch the STL completely, but only use its freestanding subset. Implementations contain some very fast SIMD-accelerated code[1]. +The STL works without exceptions.

[1]: https://github.com/microsoft/STL/blob/main/stl/src/vector_al...

Top #3 — pron:

Also, Zig is as at least as expressive as C++ (but without the implicitness and general language complexity that makes reviewing some sensitive code, where you need to see exactly what operations are performed, hard), and it supports arenas better than C/C++/Rust.

↳ reply — coolThingsFirst:

show me operator overloading in Zig

↳↳ reply — pron:

In critical low-level code, any kind of overloading - operator or otherwise - is something you'd rather not have.

By expressivity I don't mean what characters you use in the conrecte syntax, but the number of lines needed to express an algorithm (up to a small constant). C doesn't have C++'s expressivity because it lacks templates, and while you can sort of express that kind of thing with macros, it's not all the way there. Zig, however, gets you all the way there (you might need to write matrix_plus instead of +, but the expressivity is the same).

↳↳↳ reply — Ygg2:

BS. Using operator overloading with SIMD makes it easier to translate algorithms into code. I wrote my own U8x32 wrappers and a + b is way better than a.add(b).

Here was the magic that Switcher introduced.

Open up Multiplan, and fire up some spreadsheet manifestation.

Then, launch Cricket Graph as the second app.

Go back to Multiplan, click on a column, Cmd-C to copy it, switch back to Cricket Graph and hit paste.

Voila! A new chart!

Now fire up MacDraw as a third app.

Back in Cricket Graph, Cmd-C the chart.

Switch to MacDraw, and Paste. Now the chart is in MacDraw. Not only is it in MacDraw, you can ungroup it and play with the primitives (the wedges of a pie, the bars of a chart, the legend as text and filled in boxes).

The magic here was that none of these applications were cooperating. It's not that they knew about each other. It was just the dumb luck of supporting common formats on the clipboard. Lines of numbers from Multiplan. A Quickdraw PICT resource from Cricket Graph.

It’s just hard today to appreciate how extraordinary that kind of painless integration was. None of these applications knew about Switcher, they all came out before it (mind, stuff was moving REALLY FAST back then).

And, how, much, much later, I tried to Copy and Paste a diagram from Visio into PowerPoint -- and it didn't work. That was a dark time.

I don't agree that "its obviously true that it was the right move". Instead of demoting Pluto, they could have promoted Ceres, and let Eris, Haumea, Makemake, etc, be planets too. Under that proposal, they could even have the category of "dwarf planets" encompassing them, it is just that "dwarf planet" would be a subcategory of planets rather than a disjoint category from them.

↳↳ reply — delta_p_delta_x:

Classifications are useful. Even the 'proper' planets we split into terrestrials, Jovian giants, and ice giants. Each planet is individually interesting in itself. One might even argue all of the bodies in the Solar System exist on a continuum of mass from the tiniest mote of space dust, to rocks and asteroids, to moons and dwarf planets to terrestrial planets, ice giants, giants, and then the Sun, and then hypergiant stars, neutron stars, black holes, and then supermassive black holes, so let's call all of them 'celestial objects'—which we kind of do. But such a catch-all is pointless. Each object behaves very differently, with wildly different physical laws governing its interior and its neighbourhood.

Classifications impose structure on a collection of celestial objects, and we can derive relationships, commonalities, understand their development, the physics governing these objects, and build useful physical and mathematical models to widen our understanding of the universe.

Most reasonable scientists understand that some of these objects will blur the edges—like many moons being more massive and larger than Mercury. Or like the largest super-Earth exoplanets being nearly as massive as Neptune, or the largest gas giant exoplanets being 30-80 times as massive as Jupiter and hence having a surface temperature of ~2000 K. But that is part of science, and possibly even where the most interesting work is.

If a massive object came into the solar system and perturbed orbits, caused chaos and collisions, then any "planet" with debris within its neighborhood would cease to be a planet. Does it realistically outweigh decades or centuries of peoples intuition of the existing definition? Its not just a matter of science, but language and communication. If you want greater specificity, come up with a new term or use compounded terms.

It very much seems like the definition was just shoe-horned to stem any more planets needing to be added. It would be interesting to know if astronomers walk the walk when it comes the definition. If I research when planets were formed would I get the date when their neighborhoods were cleared? Do discussions around large events that send debris into the neighborhood of planets correctly reflect that they cease to be planets until it is cleared?

Alan Stern said it best

>"We're going to call it a cow, except when it's in a herd." A river is a river, independent of whether there are other rivers nearby. In science, we call things what they are based on their attributes, not what they're next to.

>And the IAU definition is even worse, because it produces different categorizations for identical objects, depending on where they are. Get this — Earth at the same distance from the sun [as Pluto] would not be a planet by the IAU’s measure, because Earth can’t clear that zone either. I would say any definition that produces a result where Earth is not a planet under any circumstance is immediately indicted as ridiculous, because one thing we all agree is a planet is planet Earth!

No, they exist on a spectrum or line that is not less or more. Maybe less or more evil, maybe less or more aged or fancy. But in high fantasy you can't demote a elf to be a dwarf or a human into an orc. |

item.title: Our software engineering interviews are changing a little
item.description: 152 points, 145 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (blog.janestreet.com)

Top #1 — fernandotakai:

so, i've gone through a bunch of iterations on how to interview in days of LLMs and i came up with a process that is quite good:

first, a coding problem that is solved live (right now, online) -- it's not a hard one and most LLMs can easily one shot it.

BUT: if you are not a senior developer, you need to do it without LLM, and if you are a senior+ and do it via LLM, the bar is super raised and now you need to explain in details everything the LLM wrote as if you wrote it yourself.

the main component here is to know if the candidate understands coding in general, understands problem solving and how to dive into an existing (although quite small) codebase. solving the problem is not really the goal -- in fact, most candidates we hired did not solve it 100%, but were able to understand and explain everything that they put it on code. this usually takes 1h30.

(we also ask the candidate to open a PR against the repo just to see if they know the basics of git -- you would be surprise how many people cannot do it).

the second is an architecture interview, where we build a system together BUT instead of doing the whole spec, miro board, whatever, we do it in more of a free way: we start with a really simple, MVP level, spec and we ask how the candidate would build it. then, we add another feature, and we ask how they would go for it. during this whole thing, i ask random questions like "why would you use x instead of y?" or "why do you prefer this approach?".

one important thing: we allow the candidate to say "i don't know" and we tell the candidate that there's no gotcha questions (which is true, i hate these kind of questions). this lets the candidate be super comfortable (feedback we had from real people).

in general, this flow helped us a ton and i really really like running it :)

(edit: spelling)

↳ reply 1 — saghm:

I feel like git operations are one of the few things that I truly don't care at all about whether someone uses an LLM for and doesn't tell me. PR descriptions and commit messages should be written by humans for humans, but like, if someone doesn't know how to manually configure their git remotes and what exact command to use to amend/squash their commits into the shape needed and instead has an agent prepare all that and use the GitHub CLI to open the PR, why should I care? Beyond the code itself, I care about the things that will continue existing in the long run fitting my team's conventions (the number of commits, the commit messages, the PR description and comments, and then whether there's a merge commit at the end), but the process used to create those things doesn't matter to me.

↳↳ reply — astonex:

> but like, if someone doesn't know how to manually configure their git remotes and what exact command to use to amend/squash their commits into the shape needed and instead has an agent prepare all that and use the GitHub CLI to open the PR, why should I care?

Because LLMs aren't a reason to not learn your tools. A determinist CLI command vs using a statistical machine for it. It's just a waste of tokens at the very least.

↳↳↳ reply — saghm:

No, the reason not to learn your tools is if they're not your tools anymore, and something else is. I don't spend time trying to manually invoke filesystem APIs to create files in my work projects and instead will often just have my LSP do it when I declare a module and the file isn't found. I could memorize the exact sequence of system calls needed, but my employer would prefer I spend time on things that are more worthwhile to them.

I don't disagree that having a deterministic CLI is useful, but I'd argue that's not the question here, because the CLI is what the statistical machine will be using. The question is whether the time spent doing it manually is worthwhile compared to the tokens spent on it. I'd further argue that if you instead learn how to pick the right model for the right job so that you don't use something way more expensive than needed for the task at hand, the token overhead will be extremely minimal for stuff like git operations; knowing that you can use something cheaper than like, Astra or Opus if all you want to do is a quick git cleanup and push is going to save your employer a lot more money in the long run than if you insist on doing every messy rebase by hand.

↳ reply 2 — bluGill:

Git is a simple tool. I expect any engineer can learn to use it. While git is common, I would not expect an engineer who worked at a company using a different version control system to know how to use git (which is a really awful - I still miss mercurial). I expect you to know the general concept of version control, but the specific on is a tool I expect you can learn quickly.

↳ reply 3 — SkyPuncher:

I run a live coding challenge on a rather benign coding problem with the explicit expectation that candidates will use an LLM.

Interestingly, an LLM involved feels like it’s made it easier to assess candidates. Senior candidates know exactly what they’re doing and strongly driving the LLM. They pre-communicating design decisions, gotchas, and requirements. They also ask a lot of clarifying questions and dial in the scope (after all not building something is better than building it).

Less experienced candidates tend to jump right in, build way too much, and stumble because they delegated all of the critical thinking to the agent. They often end up in a place where the agent doesn’t align with their vision and they can’t really reign it back in.

Top #2 — bluGill:

There are a lot of people telling you how they interview and why. Almost none of them have shown even the slightly indication that they are aware there there is scientific research on what works for an interview, much less that they apply it. They also are not showing any indication that they have done any testing - to see if their questions help hire better people.

If I said they could get equal results by picking resumes at random and hiring them without any other screening could they refute that? If so have they justified every part of their process or just one step that is useful and the rest they don't know?

↳ reply 1 — Aurornis:

> Almost none of them have shown even the slightly indication that they are aware there there is scientific research on what works for an interview,

The topic of the article is about adapting interviews in the age of LLMs.

Scientific research on interview techniques requires years of retrospective analysis after the hired employees have been evaluated in their roles for a long time.

That research does not exist on this topic. It's too new. I don't think this is a valid criticism of the actual article.

↳↳ reply — mjdiloreto:

I'd add that even those years of retrospective analysis will be insufficient, because "hiring successfully" is fundamentally about measuring membership in a particular social group. You can never pick the right observable dimensions to measure in your analysis, it will ALWAYS be lacking. Sure, you can measure work done, tenure, etc, etc, but that does not mean a hire was successful.

You might have 2 people with opposite personality traits ace the interview then get put on a team together, now all of a sudden your whole team is worse overall. That's a massive effect but your study will just see it as noise.

The reality is your best hires will just be intelligent people who belong in the group and who push the mission forward.

↳ reply — berkes:

> rewrite is functionally worse for users

I've been involved in many "rewrites". Almost exclusively, the result is worse for users at release.

Especially with "big bang releases". Where a team is working behind the scenes for months or longer, attempting to rewrite the old system "bug for bug". Releasing and then finding out that some users would "hold the space bar to make the CPU heat up, and configuring emacs to interpret that as 'control'" (XKCD 1172). First, users don't see any improvements for all the time that the new system was being built. Secondly, they get all the new stuff bundled. So while they may even get value from the rewrite, it is bundled with the stuff that makes it worse. Three new features, one new bug. And all everyone sees is that new bug.

But even rewrites where parts are swapped out and released immediately, (strangler vine pattern!) are worse for the users. They do get value fast. And in small increments. They can give feedback early. But the (much longer) period in which the replacements are implemented, is almost always one of confusion, complexity, and "having to learn new things every week". We all know the systems where "change email" is a link that leads to a form on some other site, in an old design rather than part of the "edit account" page. Because the "account service" has been extracted, but the "notification service" replacement on the backlog still.

"rewrites" are almost always for the benefit of the business, the technical team, or other internal reasons. If "benefit to the users" is a part of it, it's almost always secondary: so that we can build and release and scale new features and cool stuff for users faster than with the old legacy spaghetti debt.

Top #1 — woodruffw:

The advice here is really great (as I'd expect from Hugo), but as the maintainer of zizmor I want to note some caveats with the current iteration of workflow lockfiles:

- They only lock normal action calls. If your workflows invoke other reusable workflows, you need to keep those hash-pinned manually for now.

- Composite actions are not themselves locked. Instead, they get locked transitively through their callsites i.e. the workflows that call them. This makes any individual caller that uses lockfiles safe, but it also makes the current `gh actions-lock` default unsafe (since it removes hash-pins from the composite action itself, meaning that any external caller that invokes the action loses their transitive pinning).

- Other forms of `uses:` clauses, like Docker images, are also not currently locked via the lockfile. And the same for forms of interior mutability (like an action running `npx ...` under the hood, although the latter is fully outside of GitHub's control to prevent. But these mean that you can't assume that a fully locked Actions setup is in fact 100% immutable.

I hope they address these gaps soon, because it's otherwise an excellent (and long-awaited) feature.

It's also in the "learned retrieval" paradigm - in their case they use a teacher LLM to train a much smaller router LLM how to retrieve, using an LLM-as-a-judge based reward function.

From my own experience, these learned methods from Apple, Spotify and others, are highly relevant to hyperscale only - when you are dealing with hundreds of millions of items to choose from (or more), and require super high relevance in the top-5. For all other use cases (up to a few million items) I found that just building a BM25 index, and giving the LLM a BM25 "search tool" and casting a "wide net" wins every single time compared to learned methods (though the latter are more publishable in recsys and icml).

I guess is a trade off between speed and quality, but letting the LLM explore without a bias (based on my personal experience) seems to generally provide much better results in terms of quality for the final output.

I'm not sold; that's not to say I can't be swayed, but I've spent a lot of time building RAG solutions as a "one-size-fits-all" against codebases and I am not convinced embedding models or any of the myriad BERT implementations work well enough that they can beat out grep.

Most embedding/BERT models are far too small to truly grasp the nettles when an AI ask questions to them; and if you condition the AI to only search for really basic things, then... you're basically back to grep + regex.

You need to prune all manner of useless detritus that might gum up your matches like test files, documentation, and sidecars that semantically overlap or you're just going to match your tests. That's fine if you're building a document store for a business, but if you want a "one-and-done" solution for your codebase it's rarely good enough.

And if you do use a very large embedding model (which means it'll require running in the cloud as most company computers won't run it well), then... well, you're better off just using a language model as a subagent to scout ahead for you and elide the embedding model to begin with.

Top #1 — jsrcout:

I still remember the Byte issue on Smalltalk from 1981 [0]. To high school me it was The Future for sure. It looked so cool. I had no way to try it on the family Apple II+ [1] though.

Trying out various Smalltalk-family systems in recent years showed the advantages of implementing the entire system in one language and running it in one image. There's a refreshing coherence and predictability to everything, and pervasive simplicity instead of fractal complexity.

You can browse the entire codebase in a single window - language/compiler, math operations (except for the base primitives I believe), data structures, graphics, window system, all nicely organized. Methods, even critical ones, are mostly small, straightforward, and cruft-free. Many are just a line or two.

Smalltalk gives the developer immense power. You work directly "in the code"; your changes are live instantly. You can trivially modify the system itself - just go there and start typing. All in the same browser window. You can easily look inside any running program, change its data and even its code, and just keep going. Even now it feels futuristic.

You get powerful graphics and a window system out of the box instead of the usual story where you select OpenGL/Vulkan/GUI/DOM libraries and configure tools like make/rpm/docker/pip/npm. That's probably the most "science fiction-y" aspect by far.

In short, this was the "Jetsons" future that seemed possible back when I was getting started. The future we actually got, of course, is far less elegant and unified, and far more messy and practical. That's probably for the best. But I still love Smalltalk.

[0] https://archive.org/details/byte-magazine-1981-08

[1] https://archive.org/details/byte-magazine-1985-05/page/155 (At the time I was sad because we didn't have the extra memory it needed. Now I'm more impressed that it was even possible.)

Top #1 — MayeulC:

I feel like I am commenting this under every post mentioning fingerprinting, but is there a technical reason access to fingerprinting information (screen resolution, battery level, etc) couldn't be made to "taint" the data/code, where the browser would then refuse to send off that data? Or anonymise it and replay the code before sending the request.

Of course, there are legitimate use-cases: downloading specific assets based on client device, etc. And that's a whole can of worms of side channels to open, but that would feel like a useful additional layer of defense, and the paranoia level could be configured. The price might be subtle bugs, and/or a permission dialog that most people will ignore.

I am asking this as, from what I've seen, most websites do not need complex interactions: the battery level will be used to render a battery indicator, etc. XHRs do not usually depend on such data.

↳ reply — skaul:

If by "tainting" the data you mean subtly changing it in a way that preserves functionality while making it harder to use for fingerprinting, then this is what we do at Brave browser for many of our anti-fingerprinting protections: https://brave.com/glossary/fingerprinting/#how-can-i-prevent...

↳↳ reply — nneonneo:

I think the idea is that a given JavaScript variable/context would be “tainted” the moment it accesses those APIs; taint tracking would then be used to guarantee that tainted data couldn’t be attached to any network request. The idea here is that fingerprint-capable APIs could be used but only locally.

There’s some parallels to canvas tainting: JS is blocked from reading the pixels of any canvas that has had a cross-origin image rendered to it. This is done to enforce the same-origin policy while allowing canvases to use cross-origin images like the <img> tag can.

Unfortunately, when you can run arbitrary JS, even doing strictly local computations can likely be used to leak tainted data to a cooperating untainted context. Since you’d want the JS to still be able to do something useful with the tainted data, that resulting changes could be measured to leak the data. A more draconian measure could be to just block fetch() and similar APIs entirely after you call a fingerprinting API, but that would probably break too many sites.

↳↳↳ reply — MayeulC:

Indeed, this is what I have in mind: metadata attached to variables and js contexts, "contaminating" everything it interacts with.

There would indeed be many holes to plug, especially when considering side-channel attacks.

Thank you for the answer, this is interesting, and fuels my reflection. I had not considered some of the most common leak vectors. It seems that the main risk is that almost every API surface may get tainted fairly quickly.

To take an example: Changes to the DOM could taint that part of the DOM, and if these specific elements are accessed by another context, that would taint the context. But to reduce the collateral damage, one would need deep integration: only adding or removing elements should affect the length attribute, only the changed part of a str could be tainted, etc. That said, it might not be that complex to implement: assuming an attribute is computed by walking a list, the taint should be applied when crossing the modified boundary. If it's stored when the change occurs, it should be tainted directly.

I guess that only a prototype + corpus would give definitive answers.

The second idea I had in mind was more complex: when detecting that a tainted context is about to perform a network request, replay the context using non-fingerprinting data. Obviously it would have a performance cost. An alternative could be: every time a context get tainted, "fork" it and perform changes both in the real context and in a "parallel universe" with dummy data: use this dummy context when sending back data.

Anyway, they are just ideas. I am not in the browser space but if I was, I'd probably ask an agent to run some experiments with this.

> One of my favorite genres of psychology experiment is called something like: “the study is probably bullshit but the effect is probably real”. At the top of that heap is The Illusion of Control, a classic from 1975 and a favorite of Psych 101 classes everywhere. Usually, this study gets summarized as “people value their lottery tickets more when you let them pick the numbers vs. when you pick the numbers for them.” It’s as if people think that the mere act of picking imbues their ticket with a bit of juju, which makes them less willing to part with it.

> That would be a beautiful study, but it wasn’t the study that was actually conducted. The “lottery tickets” in question were in fact football cards, each one with a picture of a player, their team, etc. Some participants were given the opportunity to choose their football card and some had a card handed to them. Later, just before the drawing, all of the participants were asked how much it would take to buy their card back. On average, the pickers asked for $8.67, while the not-pickers said $1.86.4

> I’m sure you can see the obvious and less exciting explanation for these results: when people were given the chance, they picked their favorite players. The people who didn’t get to pick ended up with a card they liked less. This “illusion of control” effect is merely a “reality of people having preferences and acting on them” effect.5

Alternatively, people who are knowledgeable of a subject will have selfishly biased opinions about it, which they value more than unknowledgeable people will value an arbitrary stance on the subject. From experience, this seems to affect things beyond situations of chance like lotteries, and infests collaborations like businesses in ways such as Not Invented Here Syndrome or generally poor management choices that fail to consider situational factors (e.g. overarching decrees that are ineffective in certain situations/locations/applications).

This article makes an “ok” case for social science being in its infancy (I think it is in some ways, but is more mature than widely thought in others), and a very good case for most social interventions being ineffective due to their being undertaken in methodologically flawed ways.

Most interventions are embarked upon by working backwards from unproven (often political) theories and an extremely limited range of possible tools (“give money”, “take money”, “physically punish”). That leads to the mother of all searching-only-under-the-streetlight fallacies.

But that doesn’t necessarily indict the social science academy/frontiers of understanding (which, again, are plenty flawed—just perhaps not quite as stone-aged as the author suggests). Usually, it indicts the state/designers of the intervention in question. Blaming the sciences sometimes sounds like blaming car airbag designers for motorcyclist deaths.

I’m reminded of the conservation efforts for the spotted owl. Famous academic naturalists were asked to design a conservation plan that worked with logging. They did. The state replied “fine, but we need to clear-cut 90% of the forest you asked for, so make do with 10% of the habitat”. The program did poorly, but not because the academic understanding of how to address the problem was as flawed.

item.title: A great old-timey game-programming hack (2013)
item.description: 171 points, 34 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blog.moertel.com)

→ HN comments  ·  171 points  ·  34 comments

Top #1 — sehugg:

The 6502 has a more narrow and diabolical version of the 6809's PSHS trick. The BRK instruction pushes the PC and status register to the stack in three consecutive cycles, and is pretty much the only non-interrupt instruction that writes more than twice.

The Atari 2600 has horizontal object counters that you can't set directly, but they latch when you write to them, and they set the corresponding object to the X position of the beam at that cycle. Pole Position requires three of these objects to draw the left/right side of the road and center line, and they are supposed to meet at the horizon.

But the beam moves to the right 3 pixels for every CPU cycle, and writing with STA would result in each being separated by 9 pixels. What's the fix? Move the stack pointer to where the object pointers live (the 2600 maps the stack to zero page, where the RAM and registers live) and invoke BRK, making sure the BRK vector returns you to the next instruction. The object pointers are adjacent, so BRK writes to each object pointer on successive cycles, and now each of them is 1 cycle = 3 pixels apart.

Top #2 — mikewarot:

Back in the MS-DOS days, my friend Ward Christensen worked at IBM in Technical Sales Support. They had a file informally maintained that listed every single product they had for sale, in a format that could be read on a PC. He was really good at searching it with his text editor, but he wanted a MS-DOS based stand alone program to make it easy to search for his co-workers. Thus was born, PCxREF which was a Turbo Pascal based program I wrote, that included search.

My first pass at it was a naïve search using the built in string matching. Because of the size of the file, and the speed of PCs, it would sometimes take more than 30 seconds to do a search. Ward wanted it faster, much faster.

I eventually came up with an algorithm that took the text you wanted to search for, and changed it into a special kind of bit mask, table. It was a table 256 bytes long, initialized to zeros. If the first character of the string you wanted to search for was a D, then the first bit of the $44 and $64 mask would be set, to handle case sensitivity. A wildcard * was only 1 character long, but would set all bits for that character. I then used the 8088 XLAT instruction and a very small loop ingest a character of the text being searched, use that as an index into the mask table, and AND that with the existing flag in a different register, then shifted it, checking for CARRY (a match!) and looping if not zero.

It took search down to less than 3 seconds if the whole file was loaded in RAM. The thing we used as a benchmark was searching for "DOS TECH REF", the IBM DOS Technical Reference Manual.

I can't find the code, lost it over the years, but it was one of my coolest hacks.

↳ reply — gchamonlive:

These kinds of things are still important these days. In my previous employment we had to create security guardrails for content distribution resources in AWS (API gateways, s3 buckets, instances and cloudfront distros) for a standalone CDN. For cloudfront you'd be right to question why put a CDN behind a CDN and the answer is technical debt, so we had to deal with it.

The problem is that cloudfront functions are very limited in code size and execution cycles, and the list of cidr blocks from the external CDN was so long it meant we couldn't do a simple comparison, so we did something similar, representing all cidr blocks and the incoming source IP to a binary representation and used binary search to see if the source IP matched any cidr block range. It's also very hard to estimate correctly if the resulting function would in fact fit the compute budget, because AWS isn't very clear about what a cf function cycle is in practice, so we tested it extensively, with real and synthetic cases to simulate worse conditions.

Top #3 — taspeotis:

Somewhat related [1]:

> Years ago, I was working at Video Seven, a now-vanished video adapter manufacturer, helping to develop a VGA clone. The fellow who was designing Video Seven’s VGA chip, Tom Wilson, had worked around the clock for months to make his VGA run as fast as possible, and was confident he had pretty much maxed out its performance. As Tom was putting the finishing touches on his chip design, however, news came fourth-hand that a competitor, Paradise, had juiced up the performance of the clone they were developing by putting in a FIFO.

> That was all he knew; there was no information about what sort of FIFO, or how much it helped, or anything else. Nonetheless, Tom, normally an affable, laid-back sort, took on the wide-awake, haunted look of a man with too much caffeine in him and no answers to show for it, as he tried to figure out, from hopelessly thin information, what Paradise had done. Finally, he concluded that Paradise must have put a write FIFO between the system bus and the VGA, so that when the CPU wrote to video memory, the write immediately went into the FIFO, allowing the CPU to keep on processing instead of stalling each time it wrote to display memory.

> Tom couldn’t spare the gates or the time to do a full FIFO, but he could implement a one-deep FIFO, allowing the CPU to get one write ahead of the VGA. He wasn’t sure how well it would work, but it was all he could do, so he put it in and taped out the chip.

> The one-deep FIFO turned out to work astonishingly well; for a time, Video Seven’s VGAs were the fastest around, a testament to Tom’s ingenuity and creativity under pressure. However, the truly remarkable part of this story is that Paradise’s FIFO design turned out to bear not the slightest resemblance to Tom’s, and didn’t work as well. Paradise had stuck a read FIFO between display memory and the video output stage of the VGA, allowing the video output to read ahead, so that when the CPU wanted to access display memory, pixels could come from the FIFO while the CPU was serviced immediately. That did indeed help performance—but not as much as Tom’s write FIFO.

[1] https://www.jagregory.com/abrash-black-book/#the-challenge-o...

That's interesting. While the curl maintainer seems to have been underwhelmed with Mythos 5 in particular, it looks like he also backs up your account of high-quality AI reports (although unclear if these come from Glasswing or elsewhere) at this point.

> The slop is gone

> A sizeable portion of users seem to still believe we still suffer from a lot of made up and hallucinated reports by these AIs. We really don’t.

> Almost all the stupidity and lies we saw in the vulnerability reports made by AIs in the past have ceased. Since spring 2026 the slop reports are practically gone. Our current challenge is much harder: high volume, high quality.

https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2026/10/22/ignore-the-slop/

↳ reply 3 — sashank_1509:

Linux maintainer is extremely unhappy with the high false positive rate from Mythos vuln: https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=NnV_cWeoo5Q&pp=0gcJCVgCo7VqN5t...

I think someone who likes AI thinks it’s good, someone who doesn’t, doesn’t think it’s anything impressive, and concretely nothing of any significance has happened to the world, certainly nothing like the crowdstrike shutdown so I don’t find the capabilities to be anything impressive.

Top #2 — snowwrestler:

The PHP2Shell vulnerability ended up being paradoxically comforting for me.

They turned frontier models loose on PHP, and the big one they found was based on a previously known logic flaw that was extremely difficult to exploit. Which makes sense: hence the need for frontier models.

And in the wild, while there have been many attempts and a few simple demo successes, the practical impact has seemed to be small, seemingly constrained by the length of the chain and the diversity of PHP configs.

In short, it was indeed a major vulnerability, but not magic (in the Arthur C Clarke sense).

I think ultimately the fear comes down to: do you believe that code can be secured. I recognize that there is probably no objective way to deductively prove it because of the Halting Problem etc. But if one believes code can be constructed to operate to spec, then there must be a limit to the damage an LLM can do, even a very smart one.

I think we are going through a phase where a lot of known triaged code shortcomings will get exposed and hopefully fixed. Sucks while it is happening. But not actually the first round of this type of evolution. And ultimately I think as before, we will come out the other side with more secure and durable technology.

↳ reply 1 — Paracompact:

> I recognize that there is probably no objective way to deductively prove it because of the Halting Problem etc.

There is. But it will only be reliable if every transitive dependency of your codebase, all the way down to the hardware level, has been formally verified. Failing that, you have to rely on opaque contracts at the boundaries, and those are just promises that may be mistaken.

The Halting problem, Rice's theorem, etc. only apply if your goal is to automatically and completely deduce properties or their violations for arbitrary programs. If your goal is simply to prove security and correctness properties for well-understood classes of programs in industry, then there are no fundamental obstructions.

↳↳ reply — xelxebar:

Formal verification is not magic. It can execute deductive proofs, but the relevance and utility of those results is a question of human values. Spec bugs are a thing. Bad design is a thing. Out-of-scope usage is a thing. Even a halting oracle won't help with those.

↳ reply 2 — soulofmischief:

I think the more fundamental question than "can code be secured" is something along the lines of "can we properly measure the security of the various components of a sufficiently codebase". Security consultants have workflows but ultimately everything is ad-hoc and suffers from cominatorial explosion, and what's missing is the security equivalent of Lean, a real formalized effort to prove security. There have been many attempts, of course. One of the great problems of our era.

Top #3 — rurcliped:

The blog is misleading because it tries to characterize Project Glasswing's effectiveness through use of a tangentially related data source. A Project Glasswing vulnerability discovery most often occurs when a Glasswing partner points a Mythos-class model at its own, often proprietary, software. The data source (aka "ledger") is only for the Anthropic coordinated vulnerability disclosure program for open source software: in other words, Anthropic itself pointing a Mythos-class model at an OSS package, and then notifying the maintainer afterward that it had done this, and had findings to share. This OSS work is certainly useful, but the number of fixes reflects - in part - limited time availability by volunteer OSS maintainers, and Anthropic sometimes working without knowledge of the OSS project's threat model (the threat model is explicitly requested in the newer oss-scanner effort). Percentage fixed is often much higher for use of Glasswing with proprietary software, e.g., https://blog.cloudflare.com/cyber-frontier-models/ "Our research with Mythos Preview was conducted in a controlled environment against our own code; every vulnerability surfaced through this work was triaged, validated, and remediated where action was needed under Cloudflare's formal vulnerability management process."

↳ reply — geraneum:

> tangentially related data source

The used curl project as source which’s received mythos reports directly. What’s “tangential” about it?

Top #1 — Animats:

This is a "build it and they will come" project. It's not a "we put the inner loop of ML entirely in hardware" project. That would make more sense technically. You could cram a lot of little independent neural net inference units on one chip. But if it was pitched that way, the questions would be "Why isn't NVidia doing this", and "After you do it, what keeps NVidia from doing it". There are lots of people pitching "AI chips", with modest success.

The history of general-purpose massively parallel machines isn't good. From the Illiac IV to the Playstation 3, there's been dud after dud in this space. You can build them, but the users don't come. This sort of architecture is great if you have some specific problem that parallelizes, such as finite-element analysis or neural networks.

(I've used an NCube, and I kind of liked the Transputer concept. But both were dead ends.)

↳ reply 1 — jonathanlydall:

> From the Illiac IV to the Playstation 3, there's been dud after dud in this space. You can build them, but the users don't come.

From an armchair commentary perspective, my understanding was that the PlayStation 3's Cell processor had essentially two practical issues:

- It required extra talented software developers to be able to utilize the hardware to its potential.

- Almost all game makers wanted to also target the Xbox and potentially also PC which further discouraged the writing of platform specific code to truly utilize the unique capabilities of the Cell processor.

However, with AI today, it's completely possible that it changes the economics of being able to write software which can fully utilize new and novel architectures affordably.

So perhaps if the a Cell like processor was released today it would be more successful.

↳↳ reply — guenthert:

> However, with AI today, it's completely possible that it changes the economics of being able to write software which can fully utilize new and novel architectures affordably.

I'm not complete sold on that one. You will need training material. While there have been impressive results even for architectures/programming languages for which I would not have expected to be much training material to be available, there will be a minimum. I'm afraid for a new architecture unlike everything else, your AI coding assistant won't be of much help.

↳ reply 2 — adityaathalye:

Alt: What if it's a "let's build a kickass thing because we wanna, and see how far we can take it" project?

Failure is all but guaranteed---a chip is nothing without a computer-manufacturing-distributing ecosystem, which implies handsomely beating existing CPU/GPU makers, which is practically impossible.

My feeling: It is a worthwhile endeavour, in any scenario, for those building the thing.

- Boom: An "Epic win" outcome for these people would likely be exit to a leading chip maker, about a decade out from today.

- Base: Success would probably look like becoming a mini Texas Instruments type, making specialist CPUs for orgs that can build their own computers around said chip.

- Bust: Failure would likely be a fire sale into some giant IP portfolio (hopefully not a patent troll... that would be tragic).

↳ reply 3 — fanf2:

I was hoping to see something about how this new thing would be different from a GPU or NPU.

Vine is based on interaction nets, so I guess they are doing some kind of parallel graph reduction? Historically the problem with those kinds of architecture is they were used to run languages with poor locality, and the low-level execution model relied on mutation even when the higher-level languages were pure. Dunno how interaction nets address those problems.

Top #2 — tyingq:

Hmm. The story over at https://millcomputing.com/ always looked compelling.

Pitchbook shows it as "Out of Business" since 2019.

↳ reply 1 — xgk:

Distance-based ISA, which is the essence of belt-machines, is currently subject of intense R&D in Japan, see e.g.:

https://www.sigarch.org/distance-based-isa-for-efficient-reg...

↳ reply 2 — jiggawatts:

They spent way too long procrastinating, with zero silicon after decades of work.

For comparison, RISC-V started years later and had a tapeout within a year and working silicon available as a commercial product in less than seven years.

2003: Mill computing started

2010: RISC-V project started

2011: RISC-V first tapeout

2017: RISC-V production chips available in the market

2019: Mill computing dead?

Top #3 — eqvinox:

Tilera has tried and failed with a somewhat similar approach. [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilera]

Sounds like this is trying to go an order of magnitude further past that, but I'm not particularly optimistic it'll amount to much.

↳ reply — guenthert:

I'd think there have been many attempts at similar. An odd one is GA144 (GreenArrays): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GA144
